title: EventEmitter
lede: Node's classic EventEmitter, imported from events (it is no global), not the WHATWG EventTarget/Event trio. With no type argument every event takes any arguments, @types/node's default event map; a type argument is an event map of argument tuples. The on/once/emit/off surface is compiled by the compiler rather than a registered class, so instanceof answers as a compile-time constant, and every listener is held as a dynamic function. A subclass can still override any of those methods (the override wins at every call site, and super.<method>(...) reaches the built-in).

entries.name: new EventEmitter<T>() / class X extends EventEmitter<T>
entries.statusRow: new EventEmitter<T>() / extending it via class X extends EventEmitter<T>
entries.signature: import { EventEmitter } from 'events'; new EventEmitter<T>(); class X extends EventEmitter<T> {}
entries.description: Either construct a standalone emitter or root a class in one via extends — the subclass then gets the whole on/once/emit/off/removeListener/removeAllListeners/listenerCount/eventNames surface for free, and its constructor calls super(). With no T every event takes any arguments; T is an event map of argument tuples (`{ data: [chunk: string]; end: [] }`).

returns.desc: An emitter, or a subclass instance rooted in one.

differences: A subclass may override any EventEmitter method (`on`/`once`/`emit`/`off`/`removeListener`/`removeAllListeners`/`listenerCount`/`eventNames`) — the override wins at every call site (statically and virtually), and `super.<method>(...)` reaches the nearest ancestor override or the built-in dispatch. The override's declared signature isn't checked against the built-in it replaces
The type checker treats every event as taking any arguments; a typed map's event names and argument types are checked by code generation instead

entries.name: .on(event, listener) / .once(event, listener)
entries.signature: .on(event: string, listener: (...args) => void): this; .once(event, listener): this
entries.description: Registers a listener for an event; once fires at most once then detaches itself. Both are chainable, returning the emitter. The listener's parameters come from the event's declared payload type — one parameter per tuple element, a single parameter for a scalar payload, or none for a void event.

params.name: event
params.desc: Event name (a string literal for a map-typed emitter).

params.name: listener
params.desc: Callback whose params match the event's payload type.

differences: A **tuple** payload `[A, B, …]` is Node's multi-argument event — the listener takes one parameter per element (`(a, b) => …`); a non-tuple payload is a single argument (or none, for `void`). No open-ended `(...args)` beyond a declared tuple
A map-typed emitter requires a string-literal event name at every call site

entries.name: .emit(event, ...args)
entries.description: Synchronously invokes every listener registered for event, in registration order, passing along the arguments. Returns whether any listener ran. On a typed map an event takes exactly its tuple's arguments.

params.name: event
params.desc: Event name (a string literal for a map-typed emitter).

returns.desc: true if at least one listener ran.

differences: A map-typed emitter requires a string-literal event name

entries.name: .off / .removeListener / .removeAllListeners
entries.description: Detaches listeners. off and removeListener remove the most recently added matching listener, keeping the rest in order. removeAllListeners with no argument clears every event; passed an event name, it clears just that one.

params.name: event
params.desc: Event name; omitted on removeAllListeners to clear all.

params.name: listener
params.desc: The exact listener reference to remove.

entries.name: .addListener / .prependListener / .prependOnceListener
entries.signature: .addListener(event, listener): this; .prependListener(event, listener): this; .prependOnceListener(event, listener): this
entries.description: addListener is on under its other name. prependListener adds the listener before the ones already registered, so it runs first; prependOnceListener does the same for a one-shot listener.
differences: A map-typed emitter requires a string-literal event name

entries.name: .listenerCount(event) / .eventNames()
entries.description: listenerCount reports how many listeners are registered for an event. eventNames returns the names that currently have listeners, in registration order; an event whose last listener is removed drops out.

returns.desc: The listener count, or the array of event names.

differences: Event names are strings; a symbol event name is not supported

entries.name: emit('error', ...) special-case
entries.signature: .emit('error', payload): boolean  // throws if no 'error' listener
entries.description: Matches Node's one specially treated event name: emitting 'error' with no registered 'error' listener throws — the argument itself when it is an Error, otherwise an Error reading "Unhandled error. (<value>)" — so a forgotten handler fails loudly. Resolved entirely at the emit call site.

returns.desc: As emit — but throws when 'error' has no listener.

differences: A non-Error, non-string argument is rendered with `String()` in the message, where Node uses `util.inspect`

entries.name: events.once()
entries.description: Returns a Promise that resolves with the event's argument array the first time it fires.
entries.snippet:
import { EventEmitter, once } from 'events'
const ee = new EventEmitter<{ ready: [number] }>()
setTimeout(() => { ee.emit('ready', 42) }, 0)
const arr = await once(ee, 'ready') // [42]
differences: Single-value / homogeneous multi-arg events only (mixed-type tuples rejected)

entries.name: events.on()
entries.description: Registers a listener for an event; once fires at most once then detaches itself. Both are chainable, returning the emitter. The listener's parameters are any on an untyped emitter, or come from the event's argument tuple; it may take fewer parameters than the event passes.

returns.desc: An async iterator yielding each emission's argument array.

differences: A map-typed emitter requires a string-literal event name at every call site
A `function` listener can't read `this` (the emitter, in Node)
